bull.b: Arm’s licensing and royalty model supports exceptional gross margins because the company monetizes intellectual property without manufacturing chips. Strong operating and free cash flow provide resources for research, ecosystem development, and strategic expansion while reducing reliance on external financing.

Rapid Neoverse shipment growth and adoption by major cloud and infrastructure providers indicate that Arm is gaining durable share in data-center computing. A large developer ecosystem further strengthens software compatibility, customer adoption, and recurring royalty potential across future platforms.

bull.t: AGI CPU expansion and strong demand
bull.b: The AGI CPU moves Arm beyond a pure IP role into production silicon and broadens its addressable value chain in AI infrastructure. Customer deliveries and demand above the original target provide evidence of a potentially durable growth avenue alongside the established royalty model.

bear.b: Smartphones remain a major Arm end market, so weaker handset demand and memory-driven bill-of-material pressure can slow chip shipments and royalty growth. This creates a meaningful offset to data-center gains and may limit the pace of consolidated royalty expansion over coming quarters.

Demand alone may not translate into near-term AGI CPU revenue if wafers, substrates, testing, or memory remain constrained. These bottlenecks can delay customer deployments, defer royalty or silicon revenue, and make the timing of the new growth opportunity less predictable.

The initial AGI CPU margin profile is materially below Arm’s very high IP-oriented gross margins, so a larger silicon contribution could dilute consolidated profitability during the ramp. Reaching the targeted improvement depends on execution and scale over a multi-year period.
